contest: 1 Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs
position: No argument against Prop 1 was even submitted. Vote yes.

contest: 2 Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
position: Sure.

contest: 3 Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
position: Really only affects people making over $371K a year, and doesn't change the status quo. Vote yes.

contest: 4 Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns
position: We here at Goosebase support this because private financing of campaigns is a blight on society. We do, however, have reservations about the mechanics of these public funds. Vote yes.

contest: 5 Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers
position: California recalls are stupid as it is, and they can let someone without majority support replace the incumbent instead of holding a separate special election. Vote yes.

contest: 37 Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes
position: Adds fuel to housing demand without anywhere for that demand to go. It doesn't set the interest rate on these down-payment-replacing loans, and it props up home developers without enabling or requiring them to build where demand is highest. Vote no, for now.

contest: 38 Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research
position: A tough and misleading one. Without saying so outright, this measure all but guarantees that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy gets $4.2 billion (half the bond). We at Goosebase love science, but we also believe centralized decision-making outside of elected offices is a problem. Vote no.

contest: 39 Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification
position: Ridiculous additional barriers to voting that would cost tens to hundreds of millions of dollars a year. Vote no.

contest: 40 Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers
position: The tax is retroactive (it covers anyone who lived in California on January 1, 2026), so billionaires can't move to avoid it. Meta, for one, is already creating non-voting shares that can be sold without diluting Mark Zuckerberg's control; we read that as a way to raise cash for bills like this one. Vote yes and make them work for it.

contest: 41 Prohibits New State Taxes that Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes
position: Makes it harder to pass voter-approved taxes like a billionaire tax. We at Goosebase believe it should be easier to raise money for popular causes. Vote no.

contest: 42 Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes
position: Designed to make taxes like Prop 40 impossible in the future. Again, make the billionaires work for it. Vote no.

contest: 43 Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
position: Makes it harder to pass voter-proposed local taxes by raising the bar from a simple majority to two-thirds. We at Goosebase believe it should be easier to raise money for popular causes. Vote no.

contest: 44 Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services
position: A tough one to read through. It's a strict rule that might help the healthcare workers' union SEIU-UHW (the measure's sponsor) negotiate with employers, but it could also leave community clinics less wiggle room for upgrades. Tentative yes: overly strong unions would be a new problem for our generation, and we like new problems.

contest: 45 Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects
position: Another tough choice, balancing speed of construction against letting reviews and local communities assess the impacts of new construction. Voter beware: it doesn't only apply to housing, and the wording is vague enough that a data center could sue its way into the exemption. Current rules don't really have hard deadlines; Prop 45 sets them. We at Goosebase love public review, but hate scope creep and a lack of concrete deadlines a little bit more. Tentative yes.

contest: RTM Regional Transit Measure
position: It sucks that it's a regressive tax, but we can't afford to let transit go underfunded. Vote yes.

contest: A Charter Changes Affecting Various City Departments and Commissions
position: This one sucks; it's government minutiae. It bundles several Charter (i.e., SF's constitution) changes: 1. It eliminates, merges or moves some commissions out of the Charter and into city law (more Board of Supervisors control, and you still vote for those folks). 2. It lets the Board of Supervisors approve legal settlements more easily (by resolution instead of ordinance). 3. It creates a task force that meets every ten years to review the commissions. Tentative yes, because it doesn't move power into the executive. We're going to try to provide a summary table because this shit is confusing.

contest: B Establishing a Municipal Finance Corporation and a Public Bank
position: We love having a publicly controlled source of capital for loans. Vote yes.

contest: C Contributions to the Housing Trust Fund
position: Sure.

contest: D Changes to Ballot Measure Process
position: Do you hate reading all these measure summaries? This would make citizen measures four times harder to qualify: from 2% to 8% of voters' signatures (about 10,600 to 42,500). Is that a bad thing? Supporters don't think so, and the measure gives up the mayor's own power to place measures directly as a carrot. We think this is a fake reduction in executive power and a real reduction in regular people's ability to propose changes to the city charter. Vote no.

contest: E City Administrator’s Authority and Changes to City Contracting
position: Extends the mayor-appointed City Administrator's term to 10 years (from five), which spans multiple mayors, and gives the office broad power over spending and technology. Big increase in executive power. Tentative no.

contest: F Changes to Executive Branch Management
position: More government minutiae, but this time about the mayor's power: way more control over departments, including hiring and firing commission and department heads. This is actually a function we think should live under the executive, moderated by not approving all the other increases in executive power. Tentative yes.

contest: G Allowing Private Vehicles on the Upper Great Highway in Sunset Dunes Park
position: Leave the park alone. Vote no.

contest: H Parcel Tax to Fund Muni Operations
position: All the homies love Muni. Also, all the homies rent.

contest: I Changes to Real Property Transfer Tax
position: Tentative no. Locks half of the transfer-tax revenue from $10M+ property sales into specific housing initiatives and limits the Board's ability to change the tax. We at Goosebase generally don't like guaranteed spending (unless it's trains) because the demands of governance change.

contest: J Removal of Foreclosure Exemption for Real Property Transfer Tax
position: Taxes lenders that foreclose on properties (commercial and larger residential buildings; homes with fewer than five units stay exempt). Vote yes.
